c1.text: Level one: today a metal frame holds up her wings. Each wing is a big slab of marble. Look where they meet her back.

c1a.text: That's how she stands today. Not how she was built.

correction.tempting: Level one told you a metal frame holds her wings up today, so ancient builders might have done the same.
correction.truth: The frame is modern. The ancient wings needed no outside support: they slotted into a feathered bracket on her back.
correction.evidence: The Louvre's Focus guide: the wings were "attached to the back of the statue with no external support".

c1b.text: A real trick for marble. She didn't need it.

correction.tempting: Marble is heavy and brittle; marble copies of bronzes often needed bridges and props, like the Spear-Bearer's.
correction.truth: No strut. Each wing rested on a surface sloping slightly down into the body, a balance "normally only possible in bronze".
correction.evidence: The Focus guide: "a slight downward slope in the horizontal surface on which the wings rested"; "the technique was normally only possible in bronze".

c1c.text: Yes. Each wing slotted into a feathered bracket on her back, its resting surface sloping slightly down so her body took the weight. No outside support.

c1m.text: Huge marble wings, held by balance alone: a trick, the Louvre says, "normally only possible in bronze".

c2.text: Level one: her right wing is plaster, recreated in 1880–84. But fragments of the original marble wing survive. Compare the two wings as you see them now.

c2a.text: That's how it looks today. Not how it was.

correction.tempting: Wings come in pairs, and the two you see today look like a matching set.
correction.truth: The plaster is a 19th-century reconstruction. The ancient fragments show a wing raised higher and angled further back than the left.
correction.evidence: The Louvre's Focus guide: the right wing "was not symmetrical to the left wing". The plaster dates from 1880–84 (F. Ravaisson-Mollien).

c2b.text: Yes. The Louvre: fragments show the right wing "was not symmetrical to the left wing but raised higher and pointing slightly more to the rear".

c2c.text: Caution is fair: it is lost. But pieces survive.

correction.tempting: The whole right wing you see is plaster, so the original might seem gone without a trace.
correction.truth: Fragments of the original right wing survive, enough to show its angle. Restorers still add pieces: two feather fragments went back in 2014.
correction.evidence: Focus guide: "Fragments of the original wing indicate" its position. The record: "2 fragments de plume" were reintegrated in 2014.

c2m.text: The right wing you see is a restorer's version; the ancient one rose higher and swept further back.

c3.text: Look down again, at her ship. Two big boxes jut from its sides. Their outer faces, out of view here, carry oval openings in two staggered rows.

c3q.text: What were these boxes on a warship for?

c3a.text: The ram was the warship's weapon. Wrong place.

correction.tempting: A Greek warship's main weapon was its ram, and these boxes sit near the front of the ship.
correction.truth: The great ram sat on the prow at the waterline, with a smaller one higher on the stem. Both are lost here.
correction.evidence: The Louvre's Focus guide: the ram was "attached to the prow at the waterline"; "Both the ship's rams are missing."

c3b.text: Balance mattered here, but the boxes were the problem.

correction.tempting: The monument is a feat of balance, and these heavy boxes stick out on both sides. They could be counterweights.
correction.truth: The boxes copy a real ship. In the monument they needed balancing themselves, by a rear block weighing over two tonnes.
correction.evidence: The Focus guide: that missing rear block, "weighing more than two metric tons, originally acted as a counterbalance for the oar boxes".

c3c.text: Yes. Oar boxes were a new feature of Hellenistic warships: wooden boxes jutting from the hull to carry several tiers of longer, more powerful oars. The ovals are oar slots.

c3m.text: She lands on an up-to-date warship of her day, oar boxes and all, carved in marble.

c4a.text: Deep undercutting is real, as on the Venus. Not here.

correction.tempting: You saw the Venus's cloak undercut deep into one block. A sculptor this skilled could do the same.
correction.truth: Here the wind-raised cloth at the rear was a separate piece. Hellenistic sculptors began assembling the body itself from blocks.
correction.evidence: Focus guide: separate blocks, long used "for the head and other protruding parts", "began to be used for the body itself in the Hellenistic period".

c4b.text: Yes. The Louvre: "Several pieces of drapery were carved separately, including the drapery raised by the wind at the rear."

c4c.text: Plaster patches exist, but not here.

correction.tempting: Her belt area and left breast are plaster, so other parts that jut out could be too.
correction.truth: The rear drapery is ancient. It was already shown with her body in Paris before the 1880s plaster work.
correction.evidence: Focus guide: from 1866 to 1880 "only the Victory's body, with several fragments and the rear drapery added, was exhibited".

c4m.text: She was assembled from many carved parts: torso, wings, arms, feet and windblown cloth.

extends.concept: Torso and wings made separately and attached; a metal frame holds the wings today

c1q.what_you_learn: The ancient wings were cantilevered marble slabs, slotted into a feathered bracket and balanced on a slight downward slope, without external support; the iron armature is modern.

regionSources.title: Louvre, Focus: The Winged Victory of Samothrace, 'The structure of the monument'
regionSources.quote: The wings, carved from two large marble slabs and attached to the back of the statue with no external support (the reinforcements are modern), created a tricky problem of balance. The sculptor solved the problem by carving the outer face of each wing in one tier and slotting them into a sort of console decorated with feathers sculpted at the back of the main block forming the body. Moreover, a slight downward slope in the horizontal surface on which the wings rested meant that their weight was borne by the body. This remarkably ingenious solution meant that the sculptor was able to use cantilevering in a large marble work, although the technique was normally only possible in bronze.
regionSources.supports: Places the wing attachment on her back; how it worked.

c3q.what_you_learn: Oar boxes were a Hellenistic innovation carrying tiers of longer oars; the rams (lost here) sat at the prow's waterline; and in the monument the heavy oar boxes themselves had to be counterbalanced.

regionSources.title: Louvre, Focus: The Winged Victory of Samothrace, 'The base in the form of a ship'
regionSources.quote: The oar boxes jutting from the ship's sides are particularly well preserved. On the outer side, we can even make out the oval openings used as oar slots, arranged in two unaligned rows positioned one above the other.
regionSources.supports: Places the oar boxes and slots on the ship's sides.

regionSources.title: Louvre, Focus: The Winged Victory of Samothrace, 'A battleship'
regionSources.quote: The best-known of these developments was the addition of large oar boxes jutting from the ship's sides. These wooden structures could support several tiers of longer, more powerful oars.

c3a.quote: Both the ship's rams are missing. The most important weapon on a Greek battleship was its great ram, attached to the prow at the waterline, along with a smaller ram higher on the stem.
c3a.supports: The ram is real, and elsewhere.

c3b.title: Louvre, Focus: The Winged Victory of Samothrace, 'The structure of the monument'

c3b.supports: Balance was a real problem, caused by the boxes.

c3q.notes: Discrepancy to settle before release: the Focus guide counts 'seventeen blocks' in three courses; the Louvre record (and base node n4b) say 16.
